records.name: Jambi
records.current_summary: The audited sources contain no Jambi-specific finding; they set out the national framework that reaches visitors here: an October 2025 presidential decree listing "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among non-military security threats; legal gender recognition conditioned on sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval; a July 14-16 2026 wave of vigilante mob attacks on trans women across the archipelago, concentrated in Bogor where more than fifteen people were doused, stripped and beaten on camera; and 2022 wire reporting, retrieved as a fetch-time summary, of police denying mistreatment after a foreign transgender activist died in Bali custody.  Researchers describe anti-queer attitudes hardening markedly since 2016. In Jambi, the risk profile is that national climate - official framing of visibility as subversive, mob violence with weak accountability, and no criminalisation of identity itself - with no documented local ordinance or protection either way.

sources.claim: The Diplomat feature (Aug 2026): vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia in a 14-16 July 2026 wave, including over 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor with footage shared online; an October 2025 presidential decree lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; legal gender change requires sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval; provincial moral laws and Aceh caning remain the enforcement texture; a researcher documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016.
thin: no usable finding

Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Indonesia) supplies the national framework Jambi is assessed under: same-sex conduct is not criminalised in private but LGBT people have no anti-discrimination protections, the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising extramarital sex enters force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year's imprisonment on an immediate-family complaint, and legal gender recognition is conditioned on sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. The page further records Indonesia's 2016, 2022 and 2025 votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, police raids on a 'gay party' at a private villa (22 June 2025), the 11 August 2025 arrest of three men over an LGBTQ Facebook community page, and a 2025 Pew survey finding 93% of Indonesians view homosexuality as morally unacceptable. These dated national specifics corroborate and sharpen the record's 'national climate' assessment for Jambi, where no local ordinance, protection or documented incident was found in either direction.

records.name: Riau
records.current_summary: Riau's audited sources are national-level: a 2022 wire report, retrieved only as a fetch-time summary, of police denying violence in the death in Bali custody of a transgender rights activist arrested on drug charges; and an August 2026 feature recording President Prabowo's October 2025 decree listing "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among non-military security threats alongside terrorism and narcotics, and a wave of vigilante mob attacks on trans women during 14-16 July 2026, concentrated in West Java's Bogor, as the government moved to codify anti-LGBT attitudes into law.  No Riau-specific statute, raid, protection or service record appears in the material. The province is assessed under those national conditions: identity is not criminalised in most of the republic, but the official posture now treats visibility as a security threat and mob violence recurs with limited accountability; nothing documents a Riau divergence either way.

sources.claim: The Diplomat feature (14 August 2026) on Indonesia's trans community facing growing repression: President Prabowo Subianto's October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary security threats alongside terrorism and drugs; a wave of vigilante mob attacks on trans women during 14-16 July 2026, including in West Java's Bogor, followed, as the government moves to codify anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law.
thin: no usable finding

Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Indonesia) supplies the national framework under which Riau is assessed: private, consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised nationally (only Aceh applies sharia-based penalties), but Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections for sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender change on official documents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. The page records that the penal code passed in December 2022 criminalises sex outside marriage from 2 January 2026, effectively sweeping in unmarried same-sex couples since same-sex marriage is unrecognised, and that in August 2025 police arrested three men over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page with up to 12 years' imprisonment possible if convicted. This is the operative baseline a trans visitor to Riau stands under; the Riau province article itself carries no provincial divergence on any of it.

records.name: Maluku
records.current_summary: Both audited sources for Maluku are national and were only partly retrievable: a 2022 wire report on police denying mistreatment in the death in Bali custody of a transgender activist arrested on drug charges (page not retrievable; fetch-time summary), and an August 2026 feature on widening repression of Indonesia's transgender community, including vigilante mob attacks (navigation-only at fetch; headline and dossier summary).  Neither source documents any Maluku-specific enforcement, ordinance, protection or service. The province is assessed on the national picture those sources sketch: criminalisation of same-sex conduct concentrated in the one province retaining religious courts, gender recognition restricted by surgery-plus-court rules, and an official and street-level hostility climate hardening since 2016 - asserted here only at the confidence the two hedged summaries support.

sources.claim: The Diplomat (Aug 2026): Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression - vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions.

Wikipedia's national-framework overview, the position a visitor to Maluku stands under: private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised nationally, but the penal code as amended on 6 December 2022 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage effective 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within that outside-marriage restriction. Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with no third-gender or X marker; since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards (in nine provinces) as the document route. National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections and the Constitution is silent on sexual orientation and gender identity; on 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected 5-4 a petition to criminalise homosexuality, and the Sharia-based criminalisation outlier is Aceh, not Maluku. The page records that Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity and that a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.
thin: no usable finding

records.name: Sabah
records.current_summary: The audited sources for Sabah document Malaysia's federal and state-level framework rather than the province itself: same-sex conduct is criminalised under Section 377A with penalties up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and state-level syariah enactments penalise male cross-dressing; a 2022 human-rights report (retrieved as a fetch-time summary) documents state-backed discrimination - arrests, raids and prosecutions driven by state religious authorities - across the federation. The source files state expressly that they contain no unit-specific findings for Sabah.  Sabah is therefore assessed on the national framework alone: criminal provisions apply through the federal penal code as in the rest of Malaysia, religious-offence jurisdiction exists at state level, and no audited source supports treating this province as materially safer or harsher than the federal baseline.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust profile (Malaysia, last updated 16 Dec 2025) documents the federal framework this province is assessed under: same-sex 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' is criminalised under Penal Code 1936 Sections 377A/377B with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, transgender people can be targeted through the 'gross indecency' offence and state Sharia enactments prohibiting cross-dressing and 'males posing as females', with enforcement reported since the 2018 election (arrests, prosecutions, corporal punishment). The profile contains no Sabah-specific findings.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia: arrests and criminal prosecutions at federal and state-Sharia level, a crackdown persisting since the 2018 election, and the 2021 Nur Sajat case in which a transgender woman faced a religious-affairs arrest warrant and a 122-officer search. It calls for decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and gender diversity. The report contains no Sabah-specific findings, supporting the record's assessment on the national framework alone.

records.name: Sarawak
records.current_summary: Same-sex conduct is criminalised federally (penal-code provisions carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and caning), legal gender recognition is unavailable, and a dual court system applies Sharia jurisdiction to Muslims only, while no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.  A 2022 Human Rights Watch report documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events across the federation. The audited sources document no Sarawak-specific enforcement pattern, so the national framework governs what a visitor encounters here.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 16 Dec 2025): the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and acts of 'gross indecency' with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, while state Sharia enactments criminalise same-sex intimacy and 'cross-dressing' for Muslims only; no legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded and discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Enforcement documented: since the 2018 election a crackdown has been underway — Oct 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and Nov 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. The national framework governs what a visitor faces in Sarawak.

Human Rights Watch / Justice for Sisters news release, 10 Aug 2022, on the report 'I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia': 73 LGBT people interviewed across Malaysia 2018-2021; documents the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and government-run 'rehabilitation' programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021. The report names no Sarawak-specific enforcement case; the national crackdown framework applies here.
